questiontext.text:
Goal

Write three generator functions that hand out their values one at a time.

How this works in Python

Java has two ways to hand values out one at a time. The first is the Iterator interface, and it costs you a class.

class Countdown implements Iterator<Integer> {
    private int value;

    Countdown(int start) {
        this.value = start;
    }

    public boolean hasNext() {
        return value > 0;
    }

    public Integer next() {
        return value--;
    }
}

Count the moving parts. A class, a field to remember where you got to, and two methods that have to agree with each other about what "where you got to" means. Get hasNext out of step with next and you either skip a value or run off the end.

The second way is a stream, which hides the class but pushes the logic into arguments.

Stream.iterate(start, v -> v > 0, v -> v - 1);

Python needs neither. Write an ordinary function and put the word yield in its body where return would go.

from collections.abc import Iterator


def countdown(start: int) -> Iterator[int]:
    value = start
    while value > 0:
        yield value
        value -= 1

That is the whole thing. The loop counter is an ordinary local variable, and there is no second method that has to stay in step with anything.

A function whose body contains yield anywhere is a generator function. It no longer behaves like a normal function when you call it. Calling countdown(3) builds a generator object and runs not one line of the body.

The body starts running when something asks for a value. next(running) runs the body until it reaches a yield, hands that value back, and then freezes the function exactly where it stands. Local variables and the position in the loop all stay put.

Ask for the next value and the function thaws and carries on from the line after the yield. A for loop and a call to list() both do that asking for you, over and over, until the function body ends. When the body ends, next() raises StopIteration, and a for loop catches that for you and stops quietly.

The return annotation is Iterator[int], and it comes from collections.abc. Do not import it from typing, which has held a deprecated copy since Python 3.9. A generator function is annotated with what the caller receives, which is an iterator of values, not with the type of one yield.

Your task
  • countdown(start) yields start, then each number below it, down to 1. Make print("countdown is running now") the very first line of the body. The first test proves that line does not run when you call the function.
  • handshake() takes no arguments and yields three strings in order, "hello", then "again", then "goodbye". Write three separate yield statements and no loop. Each one freezes the function until somebody asks again.
  • letters(word) yields the characters of word one at a time, in order.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text exactly.

Rules
  • Do not write the word return in any of the three functions. yield is how a value leaves a generator.
  • Do not write class. Java needs one to implement Iterator, and that is the boilerplate you are here to delete.
  • Do not build a list and hand it back. No append, no list literal.
  • Annotate every signature. Import Iterator from collections.abc, never from typing.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

No AI. Type every character yourself. This tier builds the muscle, and a tool that types it for you skips the exercise.

testcode.text: running = countdown(3) print("called countdown, nothing has run yet") print(next(running)) print(next(running))

expected.text: called countdown, nothing has run yet countdown is running now 3 2

testcode.text: import inspect whole = "".join(inspect.getsource(f) for f in (countdown, handshake, letters)) assert "return" not in whole, "rule broken: yield is how a value leaves a generator" assert "class " not in whole, "rule broken: Python needs no Iterator class" assert "append(" not in whole, "rule broken: do not build a list and hand it back" assert whole.count("yield") == 5, "rule broken: one yield in countdown, three in handshake, one in letters" assert "typing" not in str(countdown.__annotations__["return"]), "rule broken: import Iterator from collections.abc" print(type(countdown(3)).__name__) print(list(countdown(0))) print(list(letters(""))) print(next(handshake()))

expected.text: generator countdown is running now [] [] hello

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write six functions, each a single return line, that work with generator expressions.

How this works in Python

The comprehensions topic gave you square brackets. Swap them for parentheses and the meaning changes completely.

[n * n for n in range(1_000_000)]        # a list comprehension, a million ints, built now
(n * n for n in range(1_000_000))        # a generator expression, no ints, built never

The first line builds a list of a million numbers and holds every one of them in memory at the same time. The second builds a generator expression, which holds the recipe and nothing else. Work that happens only when somebody asks for it is called lazy.

The size difference is not a rounding error. Ask sys.getsizeof and the list comes back at hundreds of kilobytes while the generator comes back at a couple of hundred bytes, whatever the limit is. The generator holds one value at a time, so its size never grows with the input.

Several built-in functions take a bare generator expression as their only argument. You add no brackets of your own and no call to collect a result.

sum(reading * 10 for reading in readings)
any(reading > limit for reading in readings)
all(reading <= limit for reading in readings)

Java writes those three as .mapToInt(...).sum(), .anyMatch(...) and .allMatch(...). Python matches Java on the part people forget, which is short-circuiting. any stops at the first item that passes and all stops at the first item that fails. Neither one reads the rest of the input.

Watch the empty case, because it catches people in both languages. any of nothing is False and all of nothing is True. A validator built on all therefore approves an empty batch, which is exactly what Java's allMatch does too.

Writing sum([...]) with the brackets left in still gives the right answer, so nothing tells you off. It builds the whole list first, hands it over, and throws it away. That is the million objects you meant to avoid, and one pair of characters is the only difference.

Now the part that costs data. A Java Stream cannot be reused, and it says so loudly.

IntStream evens = readings.stream().filter(r -> r % 2 == 0);
evens.count();
evens.count();
// IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed

A Python generator cannot be reused either. It is one-shot, and once something has walked it to the end it is exhausted. The difference is that Python raises nothing at all.

readings = (n * n for n in range(4))
print(list(readings))        # [0, 1, 4, 9]
print(list(readings))        # []

The second pass yields nothing. No exception, no warning, and a report that is silently blank. Java tells you on the second call, and Python leaves you to find out from the output. Reach for a list when you genuinely need two passes, and reach for a generator when one pass is all you want.

Your task
  • squares(limit) returns a generator expression yielding n * n for each n in range(limit). Return the generator itself, still lazy.
  • scaled_total(readings) returns the sum of every reading multiplied by 10.
  • any_fault(readings, limit) is True when at least one reading is above limit.
  • all_safe(readings, limit) is True when every reading is at or below limit.
  • drain_twice(values) takes one generator and returns a tuple of two lists, built by calling list(values) twice in the same return line. Python evaluates left to right, so work out what the second list holds before you run it.
  • lazy_is_smaller(limit) returns True when sys.getsizeof of the generator expression is less than sys.getsizeof of the matching list comprehension. Import sys at the top of your answer.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text exactly.

Rules
  • Never leave the brackets inside sum, any or all. A hidden test looks for sum([, any([ and all([.
  • Do not call list() in squares. It hands back something lazy or it fails.
  • Do not rebuild the generator inside drain_twice. Let the second list come back empty and read what that costs you.
  • Do not write the word for as a statement. Every one of these is one return line with the for inside parentheses.
  • Annotate every signature. squares hands back Iterator[int], imported from collections.abc and never from typing.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI for explanation only. Ask it what an error means or why one form is more idiomatic. Do not let it write your answer.

testcode.text: lazy = squares(5) print(type(lazy).__name__) print(list(lazy)) print(scaled_total([1, 2, 3])) print(any_fault([40, 12, 160], 100)) print(all_safe([40, 12, 160], 100))

import inspect whole = "".join(inspect.getsource(f) for f in (squares, scaled_total, any_fault, all_safe, drain_twice, lazy_is_smaller)) squished = whole.replace(" ", "") assert "sum([" not in squished, "rule broken: sum takes a bare generator expression" assert "any([" not in squished, "rule broken: any takes a bare generator expression" assert "all([" not in squished, "rule broken: all takes a bare generator expression" assert "list(" not in inspect.getsource(squares), "rule broken: squares hands back something lazy" assert "typing" not in str(squares.__annotations__["return"]), "rule broken: import Iterator from collections.abc" print(lazy_is_smaller(100000)) print(scaled_total([])) print(any_fault([], 100)) print(all_safe([], 100)) print(list(squares(0))) print(drain_twice(squares(0)))

name.text: WAT 14.3: The Stream That Ran Dry!

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write seven functions that keep a batch of readings lazy from end to end.

How this works in Python

Swap one character in a comprehension and the meaning changes completely.

[value for code, value in readings]        # a list, built now, all of it
(value for code, value in readings)        # a generator, built never, one item at a time

Square brackets build a list. Parentheses build a generator expression. A generator computes nothing when you write it. It computes one item each time something asks for the next one, and it forgets that item straight afterwards. Work that happens only when somebody asks for it is called lazy. A list of a million readings holds a million objects at once. The generator holds one.

You can write a generator as a function too. Put yield in the body instead of return.

def faults(readings: Readings) -> Codes:
    for code, value in readings:
        print(f"checking {code}")
        if value > 100:
            yield code

yield hands one value to the caller and freezes the function where it stands. Local variables, the loop position, everything stays put. Ask for the next value and the function thaws and carries on from the line after the yield. Java has no equivalent. There you write a class that implements Iterator, keep the position in a field, and rebuild by hand what yield does for free.

Calling faults(readings) runs none of the body. Not one line. You get a generator object back, and the first print happens only when something pulls the first value. The tests make you see that, because laziness is invisible until it surprises you.

A generator that wants to hand on the output of another generator uses yield from.

def all_faults(batches: Batches) -> Codes:
    for batch in batches:
        yield from faults(batch)

yield from faults(batch) yields every value that faults(batch) produces, one at a time, and stays lazy the whole way. Writing the inner loop by hand does the same job with more lines.

Several built-in functions accept a bare generator expression. You add no brackets of your own and no final call to collect the result.

  • sum(value for code, value in readings) adds them up.
  • all(value <= 100 for code, value in readings) is True when every item passes, and it stops at the first failure.
  • any(value > 100 for code, value in readings) is True when one item passes, and it stops there.
  • next(faults(readings), None) pulls one value and gives you None when there is none. This is how you find the first match without a loop and without a break.

A generator can be endless, because nothing has to hold it all.

def stream(start: int) -> Numbers:
    value = start
    while True:
        yield value
        value += 1

That while True never ends and the function never returns. Take a slice of it with islice from the itertools module.

from itertools import islice
islice(stream(3), 5)          # the first five values, still lazy

Now the trap that gives this exercise its name. Reuse a Java Stream and it throws IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed. You find out immediately. Reuse a Python generator and nothing is raised at all. The generator is exhausted, so it yields nothing. Your second pass produces an empty result and your report is silently blank. A hidden test drains one generator object twice and prints both results side by side.

Your task

Readings arrive as a list of (code, value) tuples, and a fault is a value above 100.

  • faults(readings) prints f"checking {code}" for each tuple it examines and yields the code of every fault. Copy the printed text exactly.
  • all_faults(batches) takes a list of readings lists and delegates to faults with yield from.
  • verdict(readings) returns a tuple of two booleans. The first is True when every reading is safe. The second is True when any reading is a fault. Build them with all and any over generator expressions.
  • first_fault(readings) returns the first fault code, or None when there is none.
  • stream(start) yields start, then start + 1, for ever.
  • first_five(start) returns the first five values of stream(start) as a lazy object, not as a list. The test prints it with print(*first_five(3)).
  • total(readings) returns the sum of the values.

Import islice at the top of your answer. The type aliases above the functions are supplied rather than written by you. A return type such as Iterator[str] needs square brackets, and the first rule below bans those inside the functions.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text exactly.

Rules
  • Do not type a single square bracket anywhere in your answer. Everything stays lazy, and a returned list is a failure.
  • Do not call list().
  • Do not try to reach the end of stream. It has none, and the checker will hang until it is killed.
  • Find the first fault with next(..., None). Do not write a loop with a break.
  • Use parentheses for the total, not brackets. One character is the difference between a million objects and none.
  • Annotate every signature out of the supplied aliases. A generator hands back an Iterator rather than a list, and the return type has to admit that.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI allowed, on three conditions. Write your plan before you open it. Read every suggestion and reject the ones you did not plan. Type accepted code out yourself rather than pressing Tab.

testcode.text: batch = [("S1", 40), ("S2", 160), ("S3", 99), ("S4", 250)] running = faults(batch) print("generator made, nothing checked yet") print(next(running, None))

expected.text: generator made, nothing checked yet checking S1 checking S2 S2
checking S1 checking S2 checking S3 ['S1', 'S3'] checking S1 checking S2 None (True, False) 0

testcode.text: import inspect whole = "".join(inspect.getsource(f) for f in (faults, all_faults, verdict, first_fault, stream, first_five, total)) assert "[" not in whole, "rule broken: not one square bracket anywhere" assert "list(" not in whole, "rule broken: a returned list is a failure" assert "break" not in whole, "rule broken: find the first fault with next(..., None)" assert "yield" in inspect.getsource(faults), "rule broken: faults must yield" assert "yield from" in inspect.getsource(all_faults), "rule broken: delegate with yield from" once = faults([("S1", 150), ("S2", 3)]) print(list(once)) print(list(once))
